items.prompt: What is a "contract" in contract testing?
choices: A concrete, versioned record of the exact requests a consumer makes to a provider and the exact response shape it expects back
A legal document signed between two engineering teams
A type definition automatically generated from the provider's database schema
A mock server's configuration file, unrelated to any real provider
items.explanation: A contract is a data file — usually JSON — that pairs exact requests with the exact response shapes a real consumer test asserted on, not a legal or documentation artifact.
items.reference:
📄 Contract — exact request + exact expected response, generated from a real test
🪞 Mock — someone's best guess at the response shape, frozen the moment it was written

Why: a contract stays honest because it's checked against the real provider on every build; a mock has no such check built in.

items.prompt: Per L1, what does a contract capture that a hand-written mock does not?
choices: It's a byproduct of a real consumer test, not a frozen guess someone has to remember to update
It captures the provider's internal database schema
It captures every field any consumer could theoretically ever want
It captures the network latency between the two services
items.explanation: A hand-written mock is a guess frozen at the moment someone wrote it; a contract is generated from an actual test run and gets re-checked against the real provider, so it can't silently drift the way a mock can.
items.reference:
📄 Contract — exact request + exact expected response, generated from a real test
🪞 Mock — someone's best guess at the response shape, frozen the moment it was written

Why: a contract stays honest because it's checked against the real provider on every build; a mock has no such check built in.

items.prompt: In L1's Scenario, both the frontend's tests and the backend's tests passed, yet production broke. What does this show about two test suites that never talk to each other?
choices: Each suite proving internal consistency says nothing about whether the two sides still agree with each other
It shows that at least one of the two test suites must have had a bug in it
It shows that end-to-end tests are never necessary for any project
It shows that mocks should never be used under any circumstances
items.explanation: Both suites were internally correct — the frontend's mock matched its own tests, and the backend's code matched its own tests. Neither suite ever checked the two sides against each other, which is exactly the gap contract testing closes.
items.reference:
📄 Contract — exact request + exact expected response, generated from a real test
🪞 Mock — someone's best guess at the response shape, frozen the moment it was written

Why: a contract stays honest because it's checked against the real provider on every build; a mock has no such check built in.

items.prompt: In contract testing terms, who is the "consumer"?
choices: The side that calls the API and depends on its response shape
The side that serves the API and must satisfy every contract
A third-party service that neither calls nor serves the API
Whichever team wrote the API's documentation
items.explanation: The consumer is the caller — a frontend, or another service — that depends on a specific request/response shape from the provider.
items.reference:
📱 Consumer — calls the API, depends on its response shape
🗄️ Provider — serves the API, must satisfy every contract written against it

Why: naming which side owns which responsibility is what makes "whose test should catch this" answerable.

items.prompt: In contract testing terms, who is the "provider"?
choices: The side that serves the API and must satisfy every contract written against it
The side that calls the API and writes a mock for it
Whichever team has more engineers assigned to the project
The company hosting the CI infrastructure
items.explanation: The provider serves the API. Its obligation, per L1, is to satisfy every contract that's been written against it by its actual consumers.
items.reference:
📱 Consumer — calls the API, depends on its response shape
🗄️ Provider — serves the API, must satisfy every contract written against it

Why: naming which side owns which responsibility is what makes "whose test should catch this" answerable.

items.prompt: Per L1, why is the contract "consumer-driven" rather than provider-defined?
choices: It's authored from what the consumer actually uses, not a provider team guessing at an abstract spec every possible consumer might need
Because the provider team is not allowed to write any tests at all
Because consumers are always right and providers are always wrong
Because it's faster to write than a provider-defined spec, with no other reason
items.explanation: Consumer-driven means the contract reflects real, actual usage by a real consumer — not an abstract spec a provider team imagines covering every hypothetical need.
items.reference:
🙋 Consumer-driven — the contract only lists fields this consumer actually reads
📋 Provider-defined spec — has to cover every field any consumer might ever want

Why: a provider can safely change anything no contract depends on — an abstract spec can't tell it what's actually safe.

items.prompt: What's the benefit to the provider of a consumer-driven contract only listing fields the consumer actually uses?
choices: The provider is free to change or drop fields no contract depends on, without breaking anything
The provider no longer needs to run any tests at all
The provider's response body becomes smaller automatically
The provider can skip writing any code, since the contract writes it for them
items.explanation: If a field never appears in any consumer's contract, changing it can't break a real consumer — the contract tells the provider precisely which fields matter and which don't.
items.reference:
🙋 Consumer-driven — the contract only lists fields this consumer actually reads
📋 Provider-defined spec — has to cover every field any consumer might ever want

Why: a provider can safely change anything no contract depends on — an abstract spec can't tell it what's actually safe.

items.prompt: What is a "broker" in contract testing (per L1)?
choices: A shared service both teams' CI pipelines publish contracts to and check verification results against
A person who negotiates API changes between two teams in meetings
A tool that automatically rewrites a provider's code to match a contract
A caching layer that speeds up API responses in production
items.explanation: A broker is infrastructure, not a person or a code generator — a shared registry both sides' CI publishes to and queries, covered in depth in L3.
items.reference:
🗂️ Broker — a shared service both sides publish contracts to and query in CI
✅ Can-I-deploy check — has this provider version verified against every consumer's contract?

Why: the broker turns "did we break someone" into a single CI answer instead of asking every team by hand.

items.prompt: Why does a broker make "can I deploy this provider version safely" answerable without a live end-to-end environment?
choices: Because it tracks, per provider version, which consumer contracts have actually been verified against it
Because it automatically fixes any contract mismatch it finds
Because it replaces the need for provider verification tests entirely
Because it runs the consumer's real application in a hosted sandbox
items.explanation: The broker's value is tracking verification history per provider version — a "can I deploy" check just queries that record instead of spinning up a live environment to find out.
items.reference:
🗂️ Broker — a shared service both sides publish contracts to and query in CI
✅ Can-I-deploy check — has this provider version verified against every consumer's contract?

Why: the broker turns "did we break someone" into a single CI answer instead of asking every team by hand.

items.prompt: What's the general lesson of L1's Scenario (the frontend's mock said `total`, the real API said `totalAmount`)?
choices: A mock that's never re-checked against the real provider can silently drift and break in production, even with every test green
Frontend teams should never write their own tests
Backend teams should always ask permission before renaming any field
Mocks are always a bad idea and should never be used
items.explanation: The lesson isn't that mocks are wrong — it's that a mock frozen at one point in time has no mechanism to notice when the real dependency it stood in for has changed.
items.reference:
✅ Frontend's tests — green, only ever asked the mock
✅ Backend's tests — green, internally consistent with its own rename
🐛 Production — order total renders undefined

Why: two green suites that never check against each other can both be right locally and still be wrong together.

items.prompt: Per L1's Scenario, why didn't the backend's own test suite catch that its rename would break the frontend?
choices: Its tests only checked that its own code was internally consistent, not that any consumer still agreed with the new field name
The backend team disabled their tests before shipping
The rename introduced a syntax error that tests can't detect
The backend's tests were run on the wrong branch
items.explanation: The backend's suite verified its own logic against its own expectations — it had no way of knowing anything about what the frontend read from its response, since nothing connected the two.
items.reference:
✅ Frontend's tests — green, only ever asked the mock
✅ Backend's tests — green, internally consistent with its own rename
🐛 Production — order total renders undefined

Why: two green suites that never check against each other can both be right locally and still be wrong together.

items.prompt: Per L1, was hand-writing a mock for the frontend's tests a bad idea in the first place?
choices: No — mocks are the right tool for isolating a unit under test from a slow or unavailable dependency; the gap is that nothing keeps the mock accurate as the provider changes
Yes — mocks should never appear in any test suite
Yes — the mock is what directly caused the field to be renamed
No — but only because JavaScript mocks are faster than mocks in other languages
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that the mock wasn't the mistake — mocks correctly isolate a unit from a slow dependency. The mistake was assuming the mock would stay accurate on its own.
items.reference:
🧪 Mocks are the right tool for isolating a unit from a slow/unavailable dependency
🕳️ The gap: nothing re-checks a mock against the real provider as it evolves

Why: contract testing doesn't replace mocking — it adds the missing re-check contract testing is built for.

items.prompt: What's the specific gap that contract testing closes, which a hand-written mock alone can't?
choices: Nothing forces a plain mock to stay accurate as the real dependency evolves — contract testing re-verifies it
Mocks are technically incapable of returning JSON
Contract testing removes the need to write any consumer-side tests at all
Mocks can only be used for GET requests, never POST
items.explanation: A mock is a snapshot with no built-in re-check. Contract testing adds exactly that missing re-check: the provider verifies its real response still matches what the contract (generated from the consumer's real test) expects.
items.reference:
🧪 Mocks are the right tool for isolating a unit from a slow/unavailable dependency
🕳️ The gap: nothing re-checks a mock against the real provider as it evolves

Why: contract testing doesn't replace mocking — it adds the missing re-check contract testing is built for.

items.prompt: Per L2, what does a contract file actually contain?
choices: A list of interactions, each pairing an exact request with the exact response shape the consumer expects back
The provider's full source code
A list of every field that exists anywhere in the provider's database
A human-readable prose description of the API, with no structured data
items.explanation: A contract is structured data — an `interactions` array of request/response pairs — not source code or free-form prose.
items.reference:
{ request: { method, path }, response: { status, body } }

Why: a contract records the exact interaction a real consumer test produced — not a hand-imagined shape.

items.prompt: Per L2, how is a contract file typically generated?
choices: By actually running the consumer's own test code against a mock provider and recording the request/response pair it asserted on
By a provider team writing it from imagination before any consumer exists
By an AI model guessing at a plausible API shape
By copying the provider's internal database schema directly
items.explanation: The contract is a byproduct of a real test run — the consumer test executes against a mock, and its actual request/response pair becomes the recorded interaction.
items.reference:
{ request: { method, path }, response: { status, body } }

Why: a contract records the exact interaction a real consumer test produced — not a hand-imagined shape.

items.prompt: What is a contract's `interactions` array a byproduct of?
choices: A real consumer test run, not a hand-written spec someone has to remember to update
A provider's automated deployment pipeline
A load-testing tool measuring response times
A static analysis of the consumer's source code, without ever running it
items.explanation: Because the interactions come from actually executing the consumer's test, the contract reflects what the consumer's code genuinely does, not a guess about what it might do.
items.reference:
{ request: { method, path }, response: { status, body } }

Why: a contract records the exact interaction a real consumer test produced — not a hand-imagined shape.

items.prompt: Per L2, what goes wrong if a provider team instead publishes an abstract OpenAPI-style spec covering every possible consumer's needs?
choices: The provider can never safely remove or rename a field without manually checking against every consumer
OpenAPI specs cannot be validated by any automated tool
Nothing goes wrong — it's strictly better than a consumer-driven contract
Consumers would be unable to make any requests at all
items.explanation: An abstract spec has to cover every field any consumer might ever want, so the provider loses the ability to tell which fields are actually safe to change without checking every consumer by hand — exactly the coordination problem contract testing exists to avoid.
items.reference:
📋 Abstract spec — must cover every field any consumer might ever want
🙋 Consumer-driven — only lists what THIS consumer actually reads

Why: the provider's real obligation is the union of what its actual consumers use, not an abstract ideal nobody can safely change.

items.prompt: Consumer A's contract only checks `id` and `status`; consumer B's contract also checks `totalAmount`. Can the provider safely rename `totalAmount` to `amount`?
choices: No — not without updating and re-verifying consumer B's contract, which explicitly depends on that exact field name
Yes, always — because consumer A's contract would still pass
Yes — because renaming a field never affects any contract
No — because renaming is never allowed once a contract exists, ever
items.explanation: Consumer A's contract would pass unchanged since it never looked at that field. Consumer B's contract encodes a real dependency on the exact name `totalAmount`, so the rename fails B's provider verification the moment it runs.
items.reference:
📋 Abstract spec — must cover every field any consumer might ever want
🙋 Consumer-driven — only lists what THIS consumer actually reads

Why: the provider's real obligation is the union of what its actual consumers use, not an abstract ideal nobody can safely change.

items.prompt: Per L2's sequence diagram, what does the consumer test suite talk to?
choices: Only a mock built from the contract itself — never the real provider
The real provider's live production database
The provider's real handler code, running in-process
A different consumer's test suite, to compare results
items.explanation: The consumer test runs entirely against a mock, which is what lets it run at unit-test speed inside the consumer's own CI without any live dependency.
items.reference:
🧪 Consumer test → talks only to a mock built from the contract
🔁 Provider verification → talks only to the real provider code

Why: neither suite needs the other side running live, which is what keeps both at unit-test speed.

items.prompt: Per L2's sequence diagram, what does the provider verification suite talk to?
choices: Only the provider's real code (in-process or a local instance), replaying interactions the contract recorded
The consumer's actual running frontend application
A mock of the provider, not the real implementation
A different provider's contract file, for comparison
items.explanation: Provider verification replays the contract's recorded interactions against the provider's own real implementation — it never talks to a mock or to the consumer.
items.reference:
🧪 Consumer test → talks only to a mock built from the contract
🔁 Provider verification → talks only to the real provider code

Why: neither suite needs the other side running live, which is what keeps both at unit-test speed.

items.prompt: Per L2, why can both the consumer test and the provider verification test run at unit-test speed?
choices: Neither one needs a live network call to the other side, or a shared environment
Because they both run on specialized, faster hardware
Because contract files are always smaller than 1 kilobyte
Because JSON parsing is faster than XML parsing
items.explanation: Both suites test against a local artifact — a mock for the consumer, the provider's own code for the provider — with no live network call between the two services, which is exactly what keeps them fast.
items.reference:
🧪 Consumer test → talks only to a mock built from the contract
🔁 Provider verification → talks only to the real provider code

Why: neither suite needs the other side running live, which is what keeps both at unit-test speed.

items.prompt: Does the provider verification test ever need to run the frontend's actual JavaScript code?
choices: No — it only needs the contract's recorded interactions and the provider's own real implementation
Yes — it must execute the frontend's rendering logic to check for visual bugs
Yes — but only during the first verification run, never afterward
It depends on which programming language the frontend is written in
items.explanation: The provider verification suite only needs the contract file (requests + expected responses) and its own real code — the consumer's code, framework, and language are irrelevant to its half of the check.
items.reference:
📄 The contract already recorded what the consumer expects
🚫 No frontend JS ever runs during provider verification

Why: the shared artifact lets the provider verify correctness for a consumer it never has to execute — even in a different language.

items.prompt: Why is it useful that provider verification never needs to run the consumer's code?
choices: It lets teams on completely different tech stacks verify against each other's expectations without running each other's code
It means provider verification tests never fail
It means the provider no longer needs to write any code at all
It removes the need for a contract file entirely
items.explanation: Since the contract is just data (requests and expected responses), a provider written in one language can verify against a consumer written in a completely different one, with no code from either side needing to run on the other's side.
items.reference:
📄 The contract already recorded what the consumer expects
🚫 No frontend JS ever runs during provider verification

Why: the shared artifact lets the provider verify correctness for a consumer it never has to execute — even in a different language.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, how does contract testing's flakiness compare to a full end-to-end test?
choices: Much lower, since there's no live network call between services
Much higher, because contract files are harder to parse than HTTP responses
Exactly the same, since both eventually check a response body
Contract testing has no concept of flakiness at all
items.explanation: Per L2's comparison table, contract tests have low flakiness specifically because there's no live network call, shared environment, or timing dependency between the two services.
items.reference:
e2e testslow, flaky, needs both services live
Contract testunit-test speed, low flakiness, no live network

Why: contract testing replaces the e2e tests whose only job was checking response shape — not every e2e test.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does contract testing NOT catch, that a full end-to-end test can?
choices: Cross-cutting issues like auth flow across calls, ordering across services, or infra problems
A response body that doesn't match what the consumer expects
A status code that doesn't match what the consumer expects
Any bug at all — contract testing catches strictly everything an e2e test does
items.explanation: Per L2's table, contract testing catches shape mismatches deterministically but is explicitly out of scope for cross-cutting issues like auth flow, ordering, and infra — L3 covers this in more depth.
items.reference:
e2e testslow, flaky, needs both services live
Contract testunit-test speed, low flakiness, no live network

Why: contract testing replaces the e2e tests whose only job was checking response shape — not every e2e test.

items.prompt: Per L2, what specific problem does contract testing solve in the test pyramid?
choices: It makes shrinking the number of expensive end-to-end tests safe, by replacing one slow cross-service test with two fast independent ones plus a shared artifact
It eliminates the need for unit tests entirely
It makes end-to-end tests run faster without changing what they check
It removes the need for any test pyramid concept at all
items.explanation: test-pyramid argues for fewer expensive e2e tests; contract testing is the concrete technique that makes that shrinkage safe, since it replaces the shape-checking job of a slow e2e test with two fast, independent tests sharing one artifact.
items.reference:
e2e testslow, flaky, needs both services live
Contract testunit-test speed, low flakiness, no live network

Why: contract testing replaces the e2e tests whose only job was checking response shape — not every e2e test.

items.prompt: Complete verifyContract(interactions, getActualResponse) so it returns { passed, failures }. For each interaction, call getActualResponse(interaction.request) and push interaction.description onto failures if the actual status doesn't match interaction.response.status, or the actual body doesn't deep-equal interaction.response.body (compare with JSON.stringify).

tests.description: matching status and body passes
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "get order 123", request: { path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999 } } }], () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999 } })).passed).toBe(true)

tests.description: body mismatch fails and is recorded
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "get order 123", request: { path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999 } } }], () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "123", total: 4999 } })).failures).toEqual(["get order 123"])

tests.description: status mismatch fails
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "missing order", request: { path: "/orders/999" }, response: { status: 404, body: null } }], () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "999" } })).passed).toBe(false)

items.explanation: This is the same check L3's real verifyContract performs, minus the file I/O — it replays every recorded interaction and reports whether the real response matches the contract, whether the mismatch is on status or on body (deep equality via JSON.stringify, since the two objects are structurally equal but different references).
items.reference:
📄 verifyContract replays each interaction against the real handler
❌ a mismatch on status OR body adds that interaction's description to failures

Why: this is the exact check that turned L1's silent production bug into a CI failure in L3's worked example.

items.prompt: Same verifyContract(interactions, getActualResponse) as before. Given multiple interactions where only some fail, confirm your implementation records exactly the failing ones and nothing else.

tests.description: two interactions, only the second fails
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "a", request: { path: "/orders/1" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "1" } } }, { description: "b", request: { path: "/orders/2" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "2", totalAmount: 500 } } }], (req) => (req.path === "/orders/1" ? { status: 200, body: { id: "1" } } : { status: 200, body: { id: "2", total: 500 } })).failures).toEqual(["b"])

tests.description: all interactions pass -> passed true, empty failures
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "a", request: { path: "/x" }, response: { status: 200, body: { ok: true } } }], () => ({ status: 200, body: { ok: true } }))).toEqual({ passed: true, failures: [] })

tests.description: all interactions fail -> both descriptions recorded
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "a", request: { path: "/x" }, response: { status: 200, body: { ok: true } } }, { description: "b", request: { path: "/y" }, response: { status: 200, body: { ok: true } } }], () => ({ status: 500, body: null })).failures).toEqual(["a", "b"])

items.explanation: Verification scans every interaction independently — one failing interaction doesn't stop the loop or hide the others, which is exactly what lets the broker section's multi-consumer, multi-interaction case report precisely which interactions broke, not just that something did.
items.reference:
📄 verifyContract replays each interaction against the real handler
❌ a mismatch on status OR body adds that interaction's description to failures

Why: this is the exact check that turned L1's silent production bug into a CI failure in L3's worked example.

items.prompt: Same verifyContract(interactions, getActualResponse) as before. Using the exact total/totalAmount rename from this unit, confirm your implementation fails against the buggy provider and passes once the provider is fixed.

tests.description: fails against the buggy provider (field is total, not totalAmount)
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "a request for /orders/123", request: { method: "GET", path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999, status: "paid" } } }], () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "123", total: 4999, status: "paid" } })).passed).toBe(false)

tests.description: passes once the provider is fixed to return totalAmount
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "a request for /orders/123", request: { method: "GET", path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999, status: "paid" } } }], () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999, status: "paid" } })).passed).toBe(true)

tests.description: the failure names the exact interaction description
tests.expr: expect(verifyContract([{ description: "a request for /orders/123", request: { method: "GET", path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999, status: "paid" } } }], () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "123", total: 4999, status: "paid" } })).failures).toEqual(["a request for /orders/123"])

items.explanation: This reproduces L3's actual before/after: the same interaction fails while the provider still returns `total`, and passes the moment the one-line fix ships — proving the fix without ever running the consumer's code.
items.reference:
📄 verifyContract replays each interaction against the real handler
❌ a mismatch on status OR body adds that interaction's description to failures

Why: this is the exact check that turned L1's silent production bug into a CI failure in L3's worked example.

items.prompt: Complete findBrokenFields(expectedBody, actualBody) so it returns an array of every key present in expectedBody that is NOT present as a key in actualBody (order doesn't matter for the tests).

tests.description: detects the total -> totalAmount rename
tests.expr: expect(findBrokenFields({ id: "123", totalAmount: 4999, status: "paid" }, { id: "123", total: 4999, status: "paid" }).sort()).toEqual(["totalAmount"])

tests.description: no broken fields when the provider adds an unrelated extra field
tests.expr: expect(findBrokenFields({ id: "1", status: "paid" }, { id: "1", status: "paid", extra: true })).toEqual([])

tests.description: detects multiple missing fields
tests.expr: expect(findBrokenFields({ id: "1", totalAmount: 1, shippingAddress: "x" }, { id: "1" }).sort()).toEqual(["shippingAddress", "totalAmount"])

items.explanation: A contract only encodes what the consumer actually depends on, so the check a provider needs before shipping a rename is exactly this: which of the fields a contract expects are no longer present at all in the new response. An extra field the consumer never asked about (like `extra` above) is never flagged — that's consumer-driven contracts working as intended, not a bug in this function.
items.reference:
📄 Contract expects: { id, totalAmount, status }
🔧 Provider now returns: { id, total, status }

Why: a field present in what the contract expects but missing from the actual response is exactly the class of change the provider needs to know is unsafe.

items.prompt: Same findBrokenFields(expectedBody, actualBody). Confirm it correctly reports nothing broken when the actual response only adds new fields, and correctly flags a field that was renamed to something else entirely.

tests.description: adding a brand-new field no contract mentions breaks nothing
tests.expr: expect(findBrokenFields({ id: "1" }, { id: "1", newField: 42 })).toEqual([])

tests.description: renaming a required field to something else entirely is flagged
tests.expr: expect(findBrokenFields({ id: "1", totalAmount: 4999 }, { id: "1", amount: 4999 })).toEqual(["totalAmount"])

tests.description: an entirely different actualBody flags every expected field
tests.expr: expect(findBrokenFields({ a: 1, b: 2 }, {}).sort()).toEqual(["a", "b"])

items.explanation: This is the provider-side question a contract answers before a rename ships: is every field a real consumer depends on still present under the same name? A brand-new, unmentioned field is always safe to add; a required field disappearing under any name is always unsafe.
items.reference:
📄 Contract expects: { id, totalAmount, status }
🔧 Provider now returns: { id, total, status }

Why: a field present in what the contract expects but missing from the actual response is exactly the class of change the provider needs to know is unsafe.

items.prompt: Complete buildContract(consumer, provider, calls) so it returns { consumer, provider, interactions }, where interactions is calls mapped so that any call missing a `description` gets one generated as `a request for ${call.request.path}`, and calls that already have a description keep it unchanged.

tests.description: generates a description when missing
tests.expr: expect(buildContract("frontend", "order-service", [{ request: { method: "GET", path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123" } } }]).interactions[0].description).toBe("a request for /orders/123")

tests.description: keeps an explicit description unchanged
tests.expr: expect(buildContract("frontend", "order-service", [{ description: "custom", request: { method: "GET", path: "/orders/1" }, response: { status: 200, body: {} } }]).interactions[0].description).toBe("custom")

tests.description: preserves the consumer and provider names
tests.expr: expect({ consumer: buildContract("frontend", "order-service", []).consumer, provider: buildContract("frontend", "order-service", []).provider }).toEqual({ consumer: "frontend", provider: "order-service" })

items.explanation: This mirrors how L3's real consumer test builds order-service.contract.json — each recorded call becomes an interaction, and a description that wasn't explicitly provided is derived from the request path so every interaction in the contract is self-explanatory without a human having written one by hand.
items.reference:
🧪 Consumer test runs → records each request/response pair it actually asserts on
📄 Those recordings become the contract's interactions array

Why: the contract is a byproduct of the consumer's own test, not something authored separately by hand.

items.prompt: Same buildContract(consumer, provider, calls). Confirm it produces exactly one interaction per call, in the same order the calls were given, without dropping or reordering any of them.

tests.description: same number of interactions as calls
tests.expr: expect(buildContract("frontend", "order-service", [{ request: { method: "GET", path: "/a" }, response: { status: 200, body: {} } }, { request: { method: "GET", path: "/b" }, response: { status: 200, body: {} } }]).interactions.length).toBe(2)

tests.description: order is preserved

items.explanation: This is exactly the property the broker section relies on when a provider has to satisfy several consumers at once — each consumer's calls become that consumer's interactions, in order, with none dropped, so provider verification can trust the contract accounts for every call the consumer's test actually made.
items.reference:
🧪 Consumer test runs → records each request/response pair it actually asserts on
📄 Those recordings become the contract's interactions array

Why: the contract is a byproduct of the consumer's own test, not something authored separately by hand.

items.prompt: Per L3's table, does contract testing catch an auth/session flow bug that spans multiple calls?
choices: No — a contract checks one request/response pair at a time, with no model of call ordering or session state
Yes — every contract automatically tracks session state across calls
Yes, but only if the broker is configured to enable it
No — because contract testing doesn't support authenticated requests at all
items.explanation: Per L3's table, contracts are stateless request/response pairs — they have no concept of "call A must happen before call B succeeds," so an auth/session bug across multiple calls is out of scope.
items.reference:
Auth/session across callsnot caught — a contract checks one request/response pair at a time
Ordering/timingnot caught — contracts are stateless snapshots
Infra (DNS, TLS, LB)not caught — verification never touches the real network path

Why: contract testing replaces shape-mismatch e2e tests specifically — it was never meant to replace every kind of integration check.

items.prompt: Per L3, with a broker in place, if a provider version satisfies 3 of 4 consumer contracts but breaks the 4th, does the can-i-deploy check pass?
choices: No — it's a single yes/no gate requiring every contract to verify, not a majority
Yes — 3 out of 4 is a passing majority
It depends on which consumer's contract failed
Yes, as long as the 4th consumer is notified manually afterward
items.explanation: The can-i-deploy check requires every contract currently recorded against production consumers to verify successfully. One failing contract is enough to block the deploy, regardless of how many others pass.
items.reference:
✅ 3 of 4 consumer contracts verified
❌ 1 of 4 fails → can-i-deploy answer is still "no"

Why: the check is a single yes/no gate requiring every contract, not a majority — one failing consumer is enough to block deploy.

items.prompt: Per L3, what does a broker's can-i-deploy check actually ask before a release?
choices: Has this exact provider version been verified against every contract of every consumer currently in production?
Has the provider team personally asked every other team if it's okay to deploy?
Has the provider's test coverage percentage increased since the last release?
Has the consumer's frontend been manually tested by a QA engineer?
items.explanation: The can-i-deploy check is exactly that one question, answered from CI results the broker already has on file — turning "did we break someone" into a single automated gate instead of a manual cross-team ask.
items.reference:
✅ 3 of 4 consumer contracts verified
❌ 1 of 4 fails → can-i-deploy answer is still "no"

Why: the check is a single yes/no gate requiring every contract, not a majority — one failing consumer is enough to block deploy.

items.prompt: Per L3's table, why is an unverified contract sitting in a repo worse than having no contract at all?
choices: It gives false confidence ("we have contract tests") while catching nothing, making the team less careful than they'd have been without it
It slows down the provider's build pipeline more than any other file would
It is technically invalid JSON and will crash the build
It automatically overwrites the provider's real response with the contract's expected one
items.explanation: A stale, unverified contract file looks like safety without providing any — the team that would have been more careful without a contract at all now trusts a check that never actually runs.
items.reference:
📄 A contract file sitting in a repo, never run in CI
⚠️ Looks like safety, catches nothing

Why: it's the verification step running on every build that catches drift — an unverified contract gives false confidence, worse than having none.

items.prompt: Per L3, what makes a contract actually catch drift, as opposed to just existing as a file?
choices: The verification step running against the real provider on every build — the file itself proves nothing on its own
The contract being formatted with proper JSON indentation
The contract being reviewed once by a senior engineer at creation time
The contract being stored in the same repository as the provider's code
items.explanation: A contract file is inert data — it's the act of replaying it against the real provider, on every build, that turns it into an actual safety mechanism instead of a document nobody re-checks.
items.reference:
📄 A contract file sitting in a repo, never run in CI
⚠️ Looks like safety, catches nothing

Why: it's the verification step running on every build that catches drift — an unverified contract gives false confidence, worse than having none.
